title: 《Assassin’s Creed Jade》重新露面，Invincible: Guarding the Globe 提振 Ubisoft 手游收入
content:
Assassin’s Creed Jade resurfaces as Invincible: Guarding the Globe boosts Ubisoft’s mobile earnings – Mobilegamer.biz
Skip to content
Ubisoft namechecked its formerly missing-in-action mobile exclusive Assassin’s Creed Jade and noted the growth of Invincible: Guarding the Globe in its latest financial results.
We have previously speculated that
Assassin’s Creed Jade had been quietly cancelled.
A Ubisoft spokesperson told us a few weeks ago that they had ‘nothing more to share’ on the title when asked about the status of the game. Ubisoft has rarely talked about the title since a flashy showing at
Gamescom 2023,
and seemingly forgot to mention the game in a recent Assassin’s Creed franchise update.
But the Tencent-made title was namechecked as still being part of Ubisoft’s plans on mobile in yesterday’s Q2 earnings call, suggesting that work continues on the long-in-development title.
CFO Frédérick Duguet explained that while PC and console remains Ubisoft’s core focus, mobile is an opportunity in the “medium to longer term”.
Invincible: Guarding the Globe drove mobile net bookings up 64% year-on-year to ~$47.1m (€43m), growing mobile’s share of the platform split to 11%, up from 5% a year ago.
Ubisoft CFO Duguet also said that while Rainbow Six Mobile was a “a very high-quality game”, the company closed the title because the long-term financial return weren’t strong enough. “We would rather put our resources on bigger opportunities”, said Duguet of the title.
Overall, Ubisoft reported Q2 net bookings of $426.4m (€389m), above its guidance of around $406m (€370m). Excluding partnerships, net bookings were up over 50% year-on-year, said Ubisoft, which cited Assassin’s Creed Black Flag Resynced as a highlight, alongside Invincible and Rainbow Six Siege.
Elsewhere in the financial results Ubisoft said that it had established an AI-focused studio called Motherbrain. And yesterday
gamesindustry.biz
reported that it also cut 166 staff at its Montreal and Quebec studios, around 4% of its staff. The layoffs “impacted employees working on projects that had recently been cancelled or significantly changed,” according to the report.
